entries.title: Background
entries.content: By 18 July 2024, the government had escalated its response in stages over the previous week. From 7 July, the Rapid Action Battalion had been deployed alongside the police; on 10 July, the Supreme Court had temporarily suspended the quota ruling for one month following legal petitions; in the days that followed, clashes had intensified across campuses and at road blockades. On the morning of 18 July 2024, the government declared a nationwide curfew and cut mobile internet and broadband, and the army, the Rapid Action Battalion, and the Border Guard Bangladesh were deployed under curfew order. The curfew and the disconnection are described in contemporary reporting as shoot-on-sight; one widely quoted metric is that mobile data would not be restored for several days, with broadband returning in stages beginning around 24 July. Reporting in this period described the measures as the most sweeping deployment of force and communications-restriction of the protest movement to that point.

entries.title: What Followed
entries.content: In the days that followed, 19 and 20 July 2024 saw the highest casualty counts of the uprising. The disconnection severely limited verification: journalists and rights monitors worked without connectivity, and figures were revised upward as access was restored. On 21 July 2024, the Supreme Court issued a ruling that scaled back the quota system. Specifically, it restored the 2018 circular: 93 percent of civil-service posts were reallocated on merit, with 5 percent reserved for the children of freedom fighters and 1 percent each for three other categories. In the days after the ruling, the curfew was eased and mobile internet was restored in stages beginning around 23 July. Reporting in this window described a relative calm compared with 18 through 20 July. The 21 July ruling closed one phase of the movement; subsequent chapters cover the period after the ruling, including matters that arose in the days and weeks that followed.
